opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the two are more connected than people sometimes assume. The way I'd put it is that a lot of the most concrete, near-term ways advanced AI could go badly run straight through biology.

When I think about what dangerous AI looks like in practice, one of the clearest pathways is AI systems that substantially lower the barrier to developing biological weapons. That could mean helping someone with modest expertise troubleshoot the steps that have historically been the hard part, or eventually helping more sophisticated actors do things nobody could do before. So a lot of the "dangerous capability" evaluations that AI companies run focus on bio, and I think that's right. It's one of the places where you can say fairly specifically what you're worried about and test for it.

That gives a couple of points of connection. First, biosecurity expertise directly feeds AI risk reduction. If you want good evaluations, good thresholds for when a model needs stronger safeguards, and good mitigations, you need people who understand the biology, the threat models, and which information really matters versus which is already widely available. There's real demand for people who can sit between those worlds.

Second, there's a defense-in-depth argument. Even if we do a great job on AI safeguards, we shouldn't assume they'll be perfect. Models leak, safeguards get jailbroken, open-weight models proliferate. So it matters a lot whether the world is resilient to biological attacks anyway: better detection and early warning, metagenomic surveillance, DNA synthesis screening, faster development and manufacturing of countermeasures, and less glamorous things like better PPE, stockpiles, and ventilation and far-UVC to cut transmission. The more robust the world is to pandemics, the less catastrophic any given AI failure becomes. In that sense, pandemic preparedness is partly an AI risk intervention.

There's also a more speculative angle. If you worry about scenarios where AI systems themselves are pursuing goals we didn't intend, biological capabilities are one of the levers that could make such a situation much worse. Hardening the world against that makes things more forgiving.

I'd add one caution. I don't think people should treat biosecurity as only a subcomponent of AI risk. Natural pandemics and non-AI-enabled misuse are serious on their own, and the field has its own norms around information hazards that AI people sometimes underappreciate. Talking loosely about exactly how a dangerous pathogen could be built, even in the name of safety, can cause harm. So I'd love to see more collaboration, but with AI people learning from the biosecurity community's caution as much as the other way around.

So, for listeners: if you have a biology or public health background and care about AI, biosecurity might be one of the highest-leverage places you can contribute, and it could matter a lot whether or not the AI picture unfolds the way I expect.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI-enabled biological threats as a concrete way advanced AI could go badly and says pandemic preparedness can reduce the consequences of an AI failure.

r002.rationale: It says AI could lower barriers to developing biological weapons, but does not clearly identify helping people release or deploy them as a pathway.

r003.rationale: It mentions AI pursuing unintended goals and biological capabilities worsening such scenarios, but does not identify AI deciding to release a bioweapon.

r004.rationale: It specifically lists better PPE as a measure that can make the world more resilient to pandemics, including those linked to AI failure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think of them as pretty deeply intertwined, and honestly that's one of the things that's shifted in my thinking over the last several years. When I first got into this stuff, I kind of treated AI and biosecurity as two separate cause areas that happened to both be in the "catastrophic risk" bucket. Now I think that's the wrong frame.

The way I'd put it is: if you ask "what are the concrete ways a very capable AI system could actually cause a global catastrophe?" — not the abstract, hand-wavy version, but the specific mechanism — biology is one of the first things that comes up. A lot of the scary scenarios for AI run through someone, whether it's a misaligned system or a human using the system, being able to design or produce something biological that's much worse than what nature or current actors could manage. So biosecurity ends up being one of the main "last lines of defense" against the ways AI could go badly.

And I think there's something nice about that, which is that a lot of biosecurity work is robustly good regardless of how the AI story plays out. If you build better early detection — metagenomic sequencing, wastewater monitoring, that kind of thing — if you build the capacity to make vaccines and countermeasures really fast, if you make PPE that actually works and is stockpiled, if you harden DNA synthesis screening so you can't just order dangerous sequences — all of that helps you if there's a natural pandemic, it helps you if there's a lab accident, and it helps you in the AI-enabled scenario. You don't have to get the forecast right. That's pretty appealing compared to a lot of the more speculative AI interventions where you're really betting on a particular model of how things go.

The other thing I'd say is that the timelines question matters a lot here. If you think transformative AI might be coming reasonably soon, then the question of "can civilization withstand a serious engineered pandemic?" becomes much more urgent, because the window where that capability might become widely accessible could be shorter than people assume. And a lot of the defensive measures take years to build out — you can't stand up a global detection system overnight. So there's a kind of race-against-the-clock element where I think biosecurity people should be thinking about AI timelines, and AI people should be thinking about what defensive infrastructure they'd want to already exist.

I'll also say that I think of this as one piece of a broader thing, which is: what does the world need to look like such that if we end up with AI systems that are much more capable than humans in various domains, that goes okay? Part of that is alignment, part of that is governance and who controls these systems, and part of that is just general resilience — making sure the specific catastrophic pathways are closed off or at least heavily defended. Bio is probably the clearest, most tractable case of that resilience work. Cybersecurity is another one. But bio is the one where I think the case is cleanest and the interventions are most concrete.

So I wouldn't say biosecurity is "an AI risk intervention" exactly, but I'd say that if you care about AI risk and you're not thinking about biosecurity at all, you're probably missing something important about how the bad outcomes actually happen.

r001.rationale: The response says biology is one of the first concrete ways a capable AI could cause global catastrophe, identifying pandemic-related biological risk as a substantial AI risk.

r002.rationale: It describes people using AI to design or produce dangerous biological agents, but does not clearly identify releasing bioweapons as the pathway to pandemic risk.

r003.rationale: It mentions a misaligned system as a possible actor in designing or producing dangerous biology, but does not say AI itself would decide to release a bioweapon.

r004.rationale: It specifically says effective, stockpiled PPE would help in an AI-enabled pandemic scenario.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a couple of connections. One is that pandemics are a major risk in their own right, and AI could make some of those risks worse. If AI makes it easier to do sophisticated biology, that could be enormously beneficial, but it could also make it easier for someone to cause a lot of harm. So improving our ability to detect outbreaks and respond quickly seems valuable across a range of scenarios, including ones where AI advances very rapidly.

The other connection is that pandemic preparedness can make society more resilient during a period when we may be dealing with a lot of other changes. You’d rather not be trying to navigate transformative AI in the middle of a devastating pandemic.

But I would distinguish that from solving the central problems of AI risk. Better pandemic preparedness doesn’t, by itself, tell us how to make AI systems reliable or how to handle the concentration of power they could create. I see it as a complementary investment: there are concrete things we can do to reduce a potentially very serious source of harm, while also working directly on AI safety and governance.

r001.rationale: The response calls pandemics a major risk and says AI could worsen them by making sophisticated biology easier, clearly identifying AI-related pandemic risk as significant.

r002.rationale: It says AI could make it easier for someone to cause harm through sophisticated biology, but does not clearly identify people releasing bioweapons as the pathway to pandemic risk.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify AI itself deciding to release a bioweapon.

r004.rationale: It discusses outbreak detection and rapid response, but does not identify deploying effective personal protective equipment as a resilience measure.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as complementary. One of the risks from increasingly capable AI is that it could make it much easier for someone to cause a biological catastrophe. So improving our ability to detect outbreaks, develop countermeasures, and keep essential systems functioning could reduce an important source of AI risk, while also helping with pandemics that have nothing to do with AI.

But I wouldn’t treat pandemic preparedness as a substitute for addressing AI risk directly. There are other ways advanced AI could cause catastrophic harm, including through our losing control of the systems themselves. Biosecurity is one area where we can build defenses against a particular pathway to catastrophe; we also need work on making AI systems safe and on governing how they’re developed and deployed.

The overlap makes biosecurity particularly attractive to me: you can do useful work against risks we already face, and some of that work could become even more valuable as AI capabilities increase.
